title: Partitioning and rebalancing
problem: After sharding, a query by anything but the shard key fans out to every shard, adding a node reshuffles data, and one hot key still pins a single partition.
summary: Local indexes make writes cheap and reads scatter-gather; global indexes invert that and go eventually consistent. Rebalance with fixed partitions, dynamic splits or per-node slices, route through a coordination service, gossip or a routing tier, and salt hot keys.
catTip: Every room in the house has its own toy box, a local index: finding the red mouse means checking all of them. One master list of toys by colour is faster to read but always a little behind where I actually dropped it.

recall.q: A photo service partitioned by user needs all photos with a given tag. Compare a local and a global secondary index for that query.
recall.a: A local index lives with each user partition, so the tag query scatter-gathers across every partition and waits for the slowest. A global index is partitioned by tag, so the query hits one partition, but each write also updates a second partition asynchronously and reads from the index are eventually consistent.

guide.breaks: Without a plan for secondary indexes every non-key query hits all shards; without a rebalancing strategy adding a node moves most of the data; without routing clients cannot find a moved partition; and a hot key saturates one partition however many you have.
guide.tradeoffs: Global indexes trade write cost and consistency for cheap reads, fixed partition counts trade flexibility for simplicity, dynamic splitting adds hot starts and background movement, and salting multiplies read work to spread writes.
guide.explainSimply: Once data is spread over many machines, new questions appear: how to find things by something other than the filing key, how to add a machine without re-filing everything, and how a request knows which machine to ask. Think of library branches: you can phone every branch, keep a central catalogue that lags a little, hand a new branch whole shelves, and spread one wildly popular book over many branches on purpose.
guide.hint: Think about where the index for a non-key attribute lives, and what a query has to do when it is not where the data is.

meow: Local index: ask every shard, meow. Global index: ask one, but it is a beat behind. Hot key? Salt it and spread the paws.

quiz.prompt: A DynamoDB table uses today's date as the partition key for event writes and is throttled at about 1,000 writes per second despite ample provisioned capacity. Which fix does the DynamoDB guide recommend?
options: Add a local secondary index on the timestamp
Write-shard the key by appending a random or calculated suffix so one day's writes spread across many partitions, merging on read
Switch the table to on-demand capacity
Create a global secondary index on the date
quiz.explanation: A single partition-key value lives on one partition with a 1,000 write-unit ceiling, and salting spreads it. More capacity or more indexes do not change which partition one key maps to.

quiz.prompt: Which rebalancing approach lets a new node take over data by adopting whole pre-existing partitions, without splitting or re-hashing anything?
options: A fixed number of partitions created at cluster start, many more than there are nodes
quiz.explanation: With a fixed oversupply of partitions, as in Riak's 64-partition ring or Elasticsearch's fixed shard count, a new node simply adopts some of them. Dynamic splitting creates partitions on size or load, and hash-mod-N remaps almost every key.

cards.q: HBase, Cassandra and MongoDB each answer the question of which node holds a key differently. Name the mechanism each uses.
cards.a: HBase: the hbase:meta catalogue table lists regions and their servers, ZooKeeper stores where hbase:meta is, and clients cache lookups. Cassandra: gossip spreads ring state to every node, and the node a client connects to coordinates and forwards. MongoDB: config servers hold the metadata and mongos routers direct client requests to shards.

cards.q: Why does a DynamoDB global secondary index offer only eventually consistent reads while a local secondary index can be strongly consistent?
cards.a: An LSI's entries live on the same partition as their base items, so a write updates both in one place. A GSI is partitioned by its own key, so base-table writes propagate to the index partition asynchronously; the index can lag, and DynamoDB therefore offers only eventual consistency on it.

glossary.note: DynamoDB's index that shares the table's partition key with a different sort key; it lives with the data, so reads can be strongly consistent.
DynamoDB's index with its own key schema and throughput, partitioned independently and updated asynchronously.
